note: Measurement only — no images are published for this entry, so nothing here is a capture claim. Our own programs on a stock C64, so no third-party rights arise and 198x/decisions/capturing-published-software.md does not bite.

measurements.tested_claim: "You'll get the same number every time... The KERNAL initialises this float to a fixed power-on value."
measurements.verdict: True, and now stated as a number the reader can check rather than an assurance. The seed at $8B-$8F reads 80 4F C7 52 58 on a cold machine and the first RND(1) is .185564016.
measurements.method: Two independent cold boots. memory_read $8B for 5 bytes on each, compared byte for byte; then PRINT RND(1) on each and the resulting screens compared. Both the seed bytes and the full screens were byte-identical across the two runs.
measurements.correction: The entry said the KERNAL initialises the seed. It is BASIC's cold-start routine that copies it from ROM, not the KERNAL. Reworded.
measurements.unverified_detail: That the ROM copy is the source was not traced through a disassembly; it is the standard account and is stated as mechanism, not as a finding. The bytes themselves were read from the machine.

measurements.tested_claim: The behaviour table's row for RND(0), which read "Repeat last number".
measurements.verdict: Wrong. RND(0) does not repeat anything. It builds a value from the CIA timers, so it differs on every call and depends on when the call happens.
measurements.method: PRINT RND(1) followed by three PRINT RND(0) on a cold machine, reading the printed values off the screen.
measurements.consequence: Four different numbers, so the row was doubly wrong: RND(0) neither repeats the previous value nor advances the sequence. The entry now says what it does instead, and notes the practical trade — it is the one form that is unpredictable from a cold start, and the one that will not reproduce when you are debugging.
measurements.also_corrected: Added that any positive argument behaves like RND(1); the value is ignored. The table implied 1 was special.

measurements.tested_claim: "RND(1) is relatively fast for BASIC—about 1500 calls per second."
measurements.verdict: Wrong by a factor of six. RND(1) manages about 245 calls a second, roughly 4.1ms each.
measurements.method: Difference of two timed loops rather than one, so BASIC's own FOR/NEXT overhead is subtracted instead of being charged to RND. Both loops are identical apart from the body: `20 X=RND(1)` against `20 X=1`. Same sentinel harness as print-vs-poke — 678 set by the program's first line, 679 by its last, both zeroed after typing, polled with memory_read every 5 frames. Granularity +/- 5 frames on each end, so about 5% on the difference.
measurements.linearity_check: Run at both 1000 and 2000 iterations specifically to test whether the figure was a per-call cost or a fixed overhead being divided by the iteration count. 244 and 247 calls/sec agree, so it is per-call.
measurements.why_this_matters_to_the_entry: The old figure made RND look cheap enough to call freely, which left the pregeneration advice further down the page looking like fussy micro-optimisation. At 4.1ms against a 20ms PAL frame, it is not: two or three random values a frame and the interpreter has nothing left. The entry now says so, and the optimisation section reads as a consequence rather than an aside.
measurements.typing_verified: chars_typed was checked against the length of each program string on every run (68/68, 63/63) because emu198x#916 makes type_string drop characters silently on the C64. Nothing was dropped; none of these programs contain an affected character.

still_unmeasured: The 'underlying algorithm' section describes RND as a multiplicative congruential generator working on the FAC float, with constants baked into the BASIC ROM. That is the conventional account and it is inherited, not verified here — confirming it means disassembling the ROM routine, which this pass did not do. The claim that the sequence period is 'long enough that no game will exhaust it' is likewise untested.
